claim: Drosophila Pumilio (Pum) and Nanos (Nos) control development, fertility, and neuronal functions.
source: We investigated combinatorial translational regulation by Drosophila Pumilio (Pum) and Nanos (Nos), which control development, fertility, and neuronal functions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of these proteins.

claim: Nanos embraces Pumilio and RNA in the Nos-Pum-RNA complex.
source: Crystal structures of Nos-Pum-RNA complexes reveal that Nos embraces Pum and RNA, contributes sequence-specific contacts, and increases Pum RNA-binding affinity.
evidence: Crystal structures are presented showing the physical interaction, and Figure 2A shows Nos enveloping Pum and RNA.

claim: Nanos contributes sequence-specific contacts to RNA in the Nos-Pum-RNA complex.
source: Crystal structures of Nos-Pum-RNA complexes reveal that Nos embraces Pum and RNA, contributes sequence-specific contacts, and increases Pum RNA-binding affinity.
evidence: Crystal structures demonstrate specific RNA contacts by Nos, shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Nanos increases Pumilio RNA-binding affinity.
source: Crystal structures of Nos-Pum-RNA complexes reveal that Nos embraces Pum and RNA, contributes sequence-specific contacts, and increases Pum RNA-binding affinity.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3E-F show that Nos increases Pum binding affinity for hb NRE2 RNA by 3-fold.

claim: Nanos shifts the recognition sequence of Pumilio.
source: Nos shifts the recognition sequence and promotes repression complex formation on mRNAs that are not stably bound by Pum alone, explaining the preponderance of sub-optimal Pum sites regulated in vivo.
evidence: SEQRS analysis in Figure 7C shows altered sequence specificity when Nos is present compared to Pum alone (Figure 7B).

claim: Nanos promotes repression complex formation on mRNAs that are not stably bound by Pumilio alone.
source: Nos shifts the recognition sequence and promotes repression complex formation on mRNAs that are not stably bound by Pum alone, explaining the preponderance of sub-optimal Pum sites regulated in vivo.
evidence: EMSAs in Figure 6A and Figure 6-figure supplements 1-2 show that Nos enables ternary complex formation with RNAs that Pum alone does not bind stably.

claim: Pumilio is a founding member of the Pum/FBF (PUF) family of eukaryotic RNA-binding proteins.
source: Pum is a founding member of the Pum/fem-3 mRNA-binding factor (FBF), or PUF family, of eukaryotic RBPs (Wickens et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wickens et al., 2002.

claim: PUF proteins share a sequence-specific RNA-binding domain known as the Pum Homology Domain (PUM-HD).
source: PUF proteins share a sequence-specific RNA-binding domain known as the Pum Homology Domain (PUM-HD) (Barker et al., 1992; Macdonald, 1992; Wharton et al., 1998; Zamore et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Pumilio binds with high affinity to specific sequences in target mRNAs.
source: Pum binds with high affinity to specific sequences in target mRNAs and represses protein expression and enhances mRNA degradation (Gerber et al., 2006; Weidmann et al., 2012, 2014; Wharton et al., 1998; Wreden et al., 1997; Zamore et al., 1999, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Pumilio represses protein expression.
source: Pum binds with high affinity to specific sequences in target mRNAs and represses protein expression and enhances mRNA degradation (Gerber et al., 2006; Weidmann et al., 2012, 2014; Wharton et al., 1998; Wreden et al., 1997; Zamore et al., 1999, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Pumilio enhances mRNA degradation.
source: Pum binds with high affinity to specific sequences in target mRNAs and represses protein expression and enhances mRNA degradation (Gerber et al., 2006; Weidmann et al., 2012, 2014; Wharton et al., 1998; Wreden et al., 1997; Zamore et al., 1999, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Regulation of hunchback mRNA by Pumilio requires collaboration with Nanos.
source: A classic example of Pum activity is the establishment of embryonic body pattern through repression of maternal hunchback (hb) mRNA, which requires collaboration with Nos (Lehmann and Nusslein-Volhard, 1987, 1991; Murata and Wharton, 1995; Sonoda and Wharton, 1999; Wang and Lehmann, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Nanos is a tandem CCHC Zn finger RNA-binding protein.
source: Regulation of hb mRNA by Pum relies on the spatial distribution of Nos, a tandem CCHC Zn finger (ZF) RBP (Barker et al., 1992; Curtis et al., 1997; Forbes and Lehmann, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Maternal hunchback mRNA and Pumilio protein are distributed throughout the syncytial Drosophila embryo.
source: Maternal hb mRNA and Pum protein are distributed throughout the syncytial Drosophila embryo (Macdonald, 1992; Tautz, 1988), whereas Nos protein forms a gradient emanating from the posterior end (Wang and Lehmann, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Nanos protein forms a gradient emanating from the posterior end of the Drosophila embryo.
source: Maternal hb mRNA and Pum protein are distributed throughout the syncytial Drosophila embryo (Macdonald, 1992; Tautz, 1988), whereas Nos protein forms a gradient emanating from the posterior end (Wang and Lehmann, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Pumilio and Nanos together repress hunchback mRNA where their expression overlaps.
source: Where their expression overlaps, Pum and Nos together repress hb mRNA (Barker et al., 1992; Lehmann and Nusslein-Volhard, 1991; Murata and Wharton, 1995; Sonoda and Wharton, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: In the absence of Nanos or Pumilio expression, Hunchback protein is produced throughout the embryo and no abdominal segments are formed.
source: In the absence of Nos or Pum expression, Hb protein is produced throughout the embryo, and no abdominal segments are formed.
evidence: This is stated as a known consequence of loss of Nos or Pum function.

claim: Regulation of hunchback mRNA by Pumilio and Nanos is dependent on two Nanos Response Elements (NREs) in the 3´UTR.
source: Regulation of hb mRNA by Pum and Nos is dependent on two Nanos Response Elements (NREs) in the 3´UTR (Murata and Wharton, 1995; Wharton and Struhl, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Each NRE contains a binding site for Pumilio with the RNA consensus sequence 5´-UGUAHAUA.
source: Each NRE contains a binding site for Pum with the RNA consensus sequence, 5´-UGUAHAUA (where H is A, U or C), the Pumilio Response Element (PRE).
evidence: This is stated as the consensus PRE sequence.

claim: Additional nucleotides in the NRE, located 5´ of the PRE, are functionally important for hunchback regulation.
source: Additional nucleotides in the NRE, located 5´ of the PRE, are functionally important for hb regulation and were proposed to be recognized by Nos (Edwards et al., 2001; Sonoda and Wharton, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Nanos by itself lacks RNA sequence specificity.
source: By itself, Nos appeared to lack RNA sequence specificity (Curtis et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Nanos binding to hunchback NREs requires Pumilio RNA recognition.
source: Instead, Nos binding to hb NREs requires Pum RNA recognition (Sonoda and Wharton, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Nanos and Pumilio collaborate to repress expression of Cyclin B mRNA in primordial germ cells and germline stem cells.
source: Nos and Pum collaborate to repress expression of Cyclin B mRNA (CycB) in primordial germ cells and germline stem cells (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999) and the sodium channel paralytic (para) in the nervous system (Muraro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Nanos and Pumilio collaborate to repress the sodium channel paralytic in the nervous system.
source: Nos and Pum collaborate to repress expression of Cyclin B mRNA (CycB) in primordial germ cells and germline stem cells (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999) and the sodium channel paralytic (para) in the nervous system (Muraro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Cyclin B and paralytic mRNAs possess NREs with PRE-like motifs.
source: Like hb mRNA, CycB and para mRNAs possess NREs with PRE-like motifs.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of these mRNAs.

claim: Genome-wide analyses have identified hundreds of Pumilio-associated mRNAs.
source: Furthermore, genome-wide analyses have identified hundreds of Pum-associated mRNAs, suggesting that Pum may play an expansive regulatory role beyond the few validated target RNAs (Gerber et al., 2006; Laver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Exogenous Nanos robustly repressed reporter protein and RNA expression in a manner dependent on the PREs.
source: We established a cell-based hb reporter mRNA assay, wherein exogenous Nos robustly repressed reporter protein and RNA expression in a manner dependent on the PREs (Figure 1) and Pum (Weidmann and Goldstrohm, 2012).
evidence: Reporter assays in Figure 1C show PRE-dependent repression by Nos.

claim: D.mel-2 cells do not express Nanos.
source: We used D.mel-2 cells, which do not express Nos and express insufficient Pum to repress the reporter efficiently in the absence of exogenous Nos (Weidmann and Goldstrohm, 2012), and a Renilla luciferase (RnLuc) reporter containing the 3´UTR of hb with two NREs, each of which possesses a PRE (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: D.mel-2 cells express insufficient Pumilio to repress the reporter efficiently in the absence of exogenous Nanos.
source: We used D.mel-2 cells, which do not express Nos and express insufficient Pum to repress the reporter efficiently in the absence of exogenous Nos (Weidmann and Goldstrohm, 2012), and a Renilla luciferase (RnLuc) reporter containing the 3´UTR of hb with two NREs, each of which possesses a PRE (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Full-length Nanos protein repressed reporter expression 75% relative to a negative control Halo-tag protein alone.
source: Halo-tagged, full-length Nos protein, comprising N-terminal, tandem ZF (Z), and C-terminal regions (NZC, Figure 1B), repressed reporter expression 75% relative to a negative control Halo-tag (Halo) protein alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1C shows 75% repression by full-length Nos.

claim: Mutation of one PRE modestly reduced Nanos-mediated repression.
source: Mutation of one PRE modestly reduced repression (Figure 1C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1C shows reduced repression with single PRE mutations.

claim: Mutation of both PREs abrogated Nanos-mediated repression.
source: In contrast, mutation of both PREs abrogated repression.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1C shows loss of repression with both PREs mutated.

claim: Nanos reduced the level of reporter mRNA.
source: Nos also reduced the level of reporter mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with enhanced degradation of target mRNAs.
evidence: Northern blot data in Figure 1-figure supplement 1 shows reduced mRNA levels with Nos expression.

claim: A single NRE is sufficient to confer Nanos-enhanced, Pumilio-mediated regulation.
source: Together, these data show that Nos-enhanced, Pum-mediated repression is PRE-dependent, and a single NRE is sufficient to confer regulation.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1C shows repression with single functional NRE.

claim: Conserved tandem zinc fingers of Nanos are necessary for RNA binding.
source: Conserved tandem ZFs are necessary for RNA binding (Curtis et al., 1997; Sonoda and Wharton, 1999), and mutations that disrupt either ZF (C319Y or C354Y) completely blocked Nos repression activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations, and Figure 1D shows loss of repression with ZF mutations.

claim: Mutations that disrupt either zinc finger (C319Y or C354Y) completely blocked Nanos repression activity.
source: Conserved tandem ZFs are necessary for RNA binding (Curtis et al., 1997; Sonoda and Wharton, 1999), and mutations that disrupt either ZF (C319Y or C354Y) completely blocked Nos repression activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1D shows complete loss of repression with C319Y or C354Y mutations.

claim: A Nanos variant lacking the C-terminal region (NZ) displayed limited repression activity (16% repression versus 79% for full-length Nos).
source: Similarly, a Nos variant lacking the C-terminal region (NZ) displayed limited repression activity, 16% repression versus 79% for full-length Nos (NZC).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1D shows 16% repression for NZ variant.

claim: A Nanos variant lacking the N-terminal region (ZC) retained 43% repression.
source: In contrast, a Nos variant lacking the N-terminal region (ZC) retained 43% repression.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1D shows 43% repression for ZC variant.

claim: No individual Nanos region (N, Z, or C) was sufficient for repression.
source: No individual Nos region (N, Z, or C) was sufficient for repression.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1D shows minimal repression by individual regions.

claim: The zinc fingers and the C-terminal region of Nanos are crucial for enhancing Pumilio-mediated repression.
source: These findings indicate that multiple regions of Nos contribute to enhancing Pum-mediated repression: the ZFs and the C-terminal region are crucial, and the N-terminal region makes a minor contribution.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1D shows that ZF and C-terminal region deletions/mutations severely impair repression.

claim: The N-terminal region of Nanos makes a minor contribution to enhancing Pumilio-mediated repression.
source: These findings indicate that multiple regions of Nos contribute to enhancing Pum-mediated repression: the ZFs and the C-terminal region are crucial, and the N-terminal region makes a minor contribution.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1D shows that ZC variant retains substantial activity while NZ has limited activity.

claim: A 3.7 Å crystal structure of the Nos-Pum-RNA ternary complex was determined.
source: We determined a 3.7 Å crystal structure that reveals the molecular architecture of the Nos-Pum-RNA ternary complex (Table 1, Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The crystal structure is presented in Table 1 and Figure 2A.

claim: The Nanos tandem zinc fingers envelop the RNA bases immediately upstream of the PRE.
source: Strikingly, the structure illustrates how the Nos tandem ZFs envelop the RNA bases immediately upstream of the PRE and, together with the C-terminal region, embrace both the RNA and Pum (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 2A and 2B shows Nos ZFs contacting upstream RNA bases.

claim: Nanos tandem zinc fingers, together with the C-terminal region, embrace both the RNA and Pumilio.
source: Strikingly, the structure illustrates how the Nos tandem ZFs envelop the RNA bases immediately upstream of the PRE and, together with the C-terminal region, embrace both the RNA and Pum (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 2A and 2B shows Nos embracing Pum and RNA.

claim: A 1.14 Å crystal structure of a binary complex of Pumilio and a hunchback PRE2 RNA was determined.
source: We also determined a 1.14 Å crystal structure of a binary complex of Pum and a hb PRE2 RNA (5´-UGUACAUA) (Figure 2C), which exemplifies the modular 1 repeat:1 RNA base recognition of classical PUF proteins.
evidence: The crystal structure is presented in Table 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: The Pumilio binary complex with hunchback PRE2 RNA exemplifies the modular 1 repeat:1 RNA base recognition of classical PUF proteins.
source: We also determined a 1.14 Å crystal structure of a binary complex of Pum and a hb PRE2 RNA (5´-UGUACAUA) (Figure 2C), which exemplifies the modular 1 repeat:1 RNA base recognition of classical PUF proteins.
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 2C shows the 1:1 recognition mode.

claim: The UGU motif of the PRE is recognized by Pumilio repeats R8 through R6.
source: For example, the UGU motif of the PRE is recognized by repeats R8 through R6.
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 2C shows this recognition pattern.

claim: Nanos binds stably and tightly to a Pumilio-hunchback NRE2 RNA complex.
source: Using an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), we demonstrated that Nos ZC binds stably and tightly to a Pum-hb NRE2 RNA complex and cooperatively strengthens the binding affinity of Pum for hb RNA.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3C-D shows tight binding of Nos to the Pum-RNA complex.

claim: Nanos cooperatively strengthens the binding affinity of Pumilio for hunchback RNA.
source: Using an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), we demonstrated that Nos ZC binds stably and tightly to a Pum-hb NRE2 RNA complex and cooperatively strengthens the binding affinity of Pum for hb RNA.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3E-F shows increased Pum binding affinity in the presence of Nos.

claim: Addition of equimolar Nanos ZC to the binding reaction further retarded the hunchback NRE2 RNA mobility, indicating formation of a Nos-Pum-RNA ternary complex.
source: The RNA-binding domain of Pum (PUM-HD) bound hb NRE2 RNA, and addition of equimolar Nos ZC to the binding reaction further retarded the hb NRE2 RNA mobility, indicating formation of a Nos-Pum-RNA ternary complex (Figure 3A,B, and Figure 3―figure supplement 1).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3B shows a super-shifted band with Nos and Pum together.

claim: Disruption of either zinc finger of Nanos (C319Y or C354Y) eliminated ternary complex formation.
source: Disruption of either ZF of Nos (C319Y or C354Y) eliminated ternary complex formation (Figure 3B).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3B shows no ternary complex with C319Y or C354Y mutations.

claim: RNA-binding deficient Pumilio mutR7 did not support ternary complex formation.
source: In addition, the Pum-hb NRE2 RNA interaction is essential for Nos binding, as RNA-binding deficient Pum mutR7 did not support a ternary complex (Figure 3B).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3B shows no ternary complex with Pum mutR7.

claim: Nanos did not shift hunchback NRE2 RNA on its own, even at protein concentrations of one micromolar.
source: Nos did not shift hb NRE2 RNA on its own (Figure 3B), even at protein concentrations of one micromolar (Figure 3C).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3B and 3C shows no binding of Nos alone to RNA.

claim: Nanos binds with high affinity to the Pumilio-hunchback NRE2 RNA complex (Kd = 4.6 nM ± 0.5).
source: We applied the EMSA quantitatively and found that Nos binds with high affinity to the Pum-hb NRE2 RNA complex (Figure 3C and D) and increases Pum binding affinity for hb NRE2 RNA by 3-fold (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3C shows Kd = 4.6 nM ± 0.5 for Nos binding to Pum-RNA complex.

claim: Nanos increases Pumilio binding affinity for hunchback NRE2 RNA by 3-fold.
source: We applied the EMSA quantitatively and found that Nos binds with high affinity to the Pum-hb NRE2 RNA complex (Figure 3C and D) and increases Pum binding affinity for hb NRE2 RNA by 3-fold (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 3E-F shows Kd of 26.3 nM for Pum alone vs 8.7 nM with Nos, a 3-fold increase in affinity.

claim: The protein-protein interactions between Nanos and Pumilio are focused between the C-terminal end of Nanos (I376Nos to E385Nos) and the non-RNA-binding convex surface of Pumilio in repeats R7 and R8.
source: The protein-protein interactions observed between Nos and Pum are focused between the C-terminal end of Nos (I376Nos to E385Nos) and the non-RNA-binding convex surface of Pum in repeats R7 and R8 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 4B shows the interaction interface.

claim: The side chain of Q1337Pum is within hydrogen bonding distance of main chain N and O atoms of I376Nos.
source: For example, the side chain of Q1337Pum is within hydrogen bonding distance of main chain N and O atoms of I376Nos.
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 4B shows this interaction.

claim: F1367Pum forms part of a hydrophobic pocket that interacts with M378Nos in the Nanos C-terminus.
source: In addition, F1367Pum forms part of a hydrophobic pocket that interacts with M378Nos in the Nos C-terminus(Figure 4B).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 4B shows this interaction.

claim: A Δ376–382 deletion of Nanos, which corresponds to the lesion in the nosL7 allele, impaired Nanos repression activity to 27% compared to 14% repression for Nos NZ.
source: We tested a Δ376–382 deletion, which eliminated much of the Pum-binding interface and corresponds to the lesion in the nosL7 allele that disrupts Nos function in vivo (Curtis et al., 1997). This deletion impaired Nos repression activity to a similar extent as deletion of the entire C-terminal region: 27% repression compared to 14% repression for Nos NZ (Figure 4C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 4C shows 27% repression for Δ376–382 deletion.

claim: Repression activity of Nanos I376A was diminished to 46%.
source: Repression activity of Nos I376A was diminished to 46%, and more so for Nos M378A (29%), whereas Nos I382A caused a modest decrease to 60%, relative to 70% repression by wild type Nos (Figure 4D).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 4D shows 46% repression for I376A mutation.

claim: Repression activity of Nanos M378A was diminished to 29%.
source: Repression activity of Nos I376A was diminished to 46%, and more so for Nos M378A (29%), whereas Nos I382A caused a modest decrease to 60%, relative to 70% repression by wild type Nos (Figure 4D).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 4D shows 29% repression for M378A mutation.

claim: Repression activity of Nanos I382A was diminished to 60%.
source: Repression activity of Nos I376A was diminished to 46%, and more so for Nos M378A (29%), whereas Nos I382A caused a modest decrease to 60%, relative to 70% repression by wild type Nos (Figure 4D).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 4D shows 60% repression for I382A mutation.

claim: A Δ383–393 deletion of Nanos diminished repression activity to 43%.
source: A Δ383–393 deletion, which removed the final three ordered residues in the structure and eight subsequent residues, also diminished repression activity to 43% (Figure 4C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 4C shows 43% repression for Δ383–393 deletion.

claim: A Δ394–401 deletion of Nanos retained full repression activity.
source: In contrast, a Δ394–401 deletion retained full repression activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 4C shows full repression for Δ394–401 deletion.

claim: The C-terminal eight residues of Nanos (394-401) were disordered in the ternary complex structure and did not contact Pumilio.
source: These C-terminal eight residues of Nos were disordered in the ternary complex structure, and therefore did not contact Pum.
evidence: The crystal structure shows disorder for these residues, and deletion does not affect repression.

claim: Pumilio F1367S mutation eliminated ternary complex formation.
source: No ternary complex was formed with Pum F1367S (Figure 4E), an R7-R8 loop mutant that binds RNA, but does not interact with Nos in a yeast 3-hybrid assay (Edwards et al., 2001) or respond to Nos in cells (Weidmann and Goldstrohm, 2012).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 4E shows no ternary complex with F1367S mutation.

claim: Pumilio Q1337A mutation eliminated ternary complex formation.
source: Similarly, a Q1337APum mutation eliminated ternary complex formation (Figure 4F).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 4F shows no ternary complex with Q1337A mutation.

claim: Both Pumilio F1367S and Q1337A mutants retained the ability to bind to hunchback NRE2 RNA.
source: Importantly, both Pum mutants retained the ability to bind to hb NRE2 RNA (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 4E and 4F shows Pum-RNA binary complex formation with these mutants.

claim: Nanos must interact with both repeat R7 and the R7-R8 loop of Pumilio to form a stable ternary complex.
source: Thus, Nos must interact with both repeat R7 and the R7-R8 loop of Pum to form a stable ternary complex.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 4E and 4F shows that mutations in R7 (Q1337A) or R7-R8 loop (F1367S) prevent ternary complex formation.

claim: The first base upstream of the PRE, -1U, is inserted into a hydrophobic binding pocket formed by F321Nos, T366Nos, and Y369Nos.
source: The first base upstream of the PRE, -1U, is inserted into a hydrophobic binding pocket formed by F321Nos, T366Nos, and Y369Nos (Figure 5A and Figure 2―figure supplement 1).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 5A shows this binding pocket.

claim: The O4 atom of −1U is near the main chain N atom of T366Nos.
source: The O4 atom of −1U is near the main chain N atom of T366Nos.
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 5A shows this interaction.

claim: Nanos contacts the bases and backbone atoms of −2A and −3A.
source: Nos also contacts the bases and backbone atoms of −2A and −3A (Figure 5B).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 5B shows these contacts.

claim: Three residues within the rearranged C-terminal region of Pumilio (T1415Pum, K1377Pum, and K1413Pum) appear to approach the phosphate groups of −2A, −3A, and −4A, respectively.
source: Three residues within the rearranged C-terminal region of Pum, T1415Pum, K1377Pum, and K1413Pum, appear to approach the phosphate groups of −2A, −3A, and −4A, respectively (Figure 2―figure supplement 1 and Figure 2―figure supplement 3).
evidence: The crystal structure in Figure 2-figure supplement 3 shows these interactions.

claim: Individual mutations that disrupted the hydrophobic binding pocket for the −1U base (F321A, T366A, and Y369A) abrogated Nanos repression activity.
source: Individual mutations that disrupted the hydrophobic binding pocket for the −1U base (F321A, T366A, and Y369A) abrogated repression activity.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 5C shows loss of repression with these mutations.

claim: Nanos K368Q mutation reduced repression activity to 32% vs 75% for wild type protein.
source: Another mutant, K368Q, designed to eliminate a salt bridge interaction with the phosphate group of −1U, reduced repression activity to 32% vs 75% for WT protein.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 5C shows 32% repression for K368Q mutation.

claim: Nanos mutations targeting interactions with nucleotides−2A and −3A (N325A and Y352A) had smaller, but measurable effects on repression activity.
source: Mutations targeting interactions with nucleotides−2A and −3A (N325A and Y352A) had smaller, but measurable effects on repression activity.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 5C shows reduced but not eliminated repression with these mutations.

claim: Substitution of cytosine at the −1 position of hunchback NRE2 blocked ternary complex formation.
source: Substitution of both the −1 and −2 positions of hb NRE2 with cytosine had been shown previously to disrupt abdominal segmentation, but did not affect Pum RNA association (Murata and Wharton, 1995), so we designed hb NRE2 RNAs that substituted cytosine bases at either the −1 or −2 position (Figure 5D, −1C and −2C). Neither mutation hindered RNA binding by Pum, but both mutations blocked ternary complex formation (Figure 5E).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 5E shows no ternary complex with −1C mutation.

claim: Substitution of cytosine at the −2 position of hunchback NRE2 blocked ternary complex formation.
source: Substitution of both the −1 and −2 positions of hb NRE2 with cytosine had been shown previously to disrupt abdominal segmentation, but did not affect Pum RNA association (Murata and Wharton, 1995), so we designed hb NRE2 RNAs that substituted cytosine bases at either the −1 or −2 position (Figure 5D, −1C and −2C). Neither mutation hindered RNA binding by Pum, but both mutations blocked ternary complex formation (Figure 5E).
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 5E shows no ternary complex with −2C mutation.

claim: Nanos did not repress mutant −1C or −2C reporters.
source: In contrast, Nos did not repress mutant −1C or −2C reporters (Figure 5F), consistent with disruption of ternary complex formation by these substitutions.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 5F shows no repression with −1C or −2C mutations.

claim: The identities of the nucleotides in the Nanos binding site are critical for repression activity.
source: Thus, the identities of the nucleotides in the NBS are critical for repression activity.
evidence: EMSA and reporter assay data in Figure 5E-F show that NBS mutations prevent ternary complex formation and repression.

claim: Pumilio alone did not form a stable complex with Cyclin B NRE RNA.
source: The Cyclin B (CycB) NRE contains a PRE that diverges from the consensus with uracils in place of adenines at positions +6 and +8, and it has a different NBS sequence (Figure 6A). Pum alone did not form a stable complex with CycB NRE RNA (Figure 6A, left, and 6B), but remarkably, addition of Nos ZC resulted in ternary complex formation with an apparent Kd of 12 nM (Figure 6A, right, and 6B), similar to the 8.7 nM Kd for hb NRE2.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 6A shows no stable Pum-CycB NRE complex.

claim: Addition of Nanos resulted in ternary complex formation with Cyclin B NRE RNA with an apparent Kd of 12 nM.
source: The Cyclin B (CycB) NRE contains a PRE that diverges from the consensus with uracils in place of adenines at positions +6 and +8, and it has a different NBS sequence (Figure 6A). Pum alone did not form a stable complex with CycB NRE RNA (Figure 6A, left, and 6B), but remarkably, addition of Nos ZC resulted in ternary complex formation with an apparent Kd of 12 nM (Figure 6A, right, and 6B), similar to the 8.7 nM Kd for hb NRE2.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 6A shows ternary complex formation with Kd of 12 nM.

claim: Pumilio did not form a stable binary complex with hunchback NRE1 RNA, but Nanos induced ternary complex formation.
source: We next tested complex formation with sequences from the hb NRE1 (Figure 6―figure supplement 1) and bicoid NRE (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), which match the PRE consensus sequence, but have a uracil or guanine, respectively, at the +5 position. For each of these sequences, Pum unexpectedly did not form a stable binary complex, but as with the CycB sequence, Nos induced ternary complex formation.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 6-figure supplement 1 shows no stable Pum-hb NRE1 complex but ternary complex formation with Nos.

claim: Pumilio did not form a stable binary complex with bicoid NRE RNA, but Nanos induced ternary complex formation.
source: We next tested complex formation with sequences from the hb NRE1 (Figure 6―figure supplement 1) and bicoid NRE (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), which match the PRE consensus sequence, but have a uracil or guanine, respectively, at the +5 position. For each of these sequences, Pum unexpectedly did not form a stable binary complex, but as with the CycB sequence, Nos induced ternary complex formation.
evidence: EMSA data in Figure 6-figure supplement 2 shows no stable Pum-bicoid NRE complex but ternary complex formation with Nos.

claim: A 4.0 Å crystal structure of a ternary complex with a Cyclin B NRE RNA was determined.
source: To gain molecular insight into how Nos enhances Pum recognition of different NRE sequences, we determined a 4.0 Å crystal structure of a ternary complex with a CycB NRE RNA (5´-UAUUUGUAAUUUAU, core PRE underlined)(Table 1).
evidence: The crystal structure is presented in Table 1 and Figure 6C.

claim: Differences in Pumilio binding to bases +5 to +8 result in distinct conformations of hunchback and Cyclin B RNAs in the ternary complexes.
source: The protein structures are essentially unchanged compared to the complex with hb NRE2 RNA; however, differences in Pum binding to bases +5 to +8 result in distinct conformations of hb and CycB RNAs in this region (Figure 6C and Figure 6―figure supplement 5).
evidence: Crystal structures in Figure 6C and Figure 6-figure supplement 5 show different RNA conformations.

claim: Pumilio binds to the hunchback PRE2 using the base-omission mode observed for human Pumilio1, where bases +4 and +5 stack directly.
source: Pum binds to the hb PRE2 using the base-omission mode observed for human Pumilio1 (Lu and Hall, 2011), where bases +4 and +5 stack directly (Figure 6D).
evidence: Crystal structure in Figure 6D shows base-omission mode with citation to Lu and Hall, 2011.

claim: Pumilio binds to the Cyclin B PRE using the 1 repeat:1 RNA base PUF recognition mode with R1271Pum sandwiched between bases +4 and +5.
source: In contrast, Pum appears to bind to the CycB PRE using the 1 repeat:1 RNA base PUF recognition mode with R1271Pum sandwiched between bases +4 and +5 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Crystal structure in Figure 6E shows 1:1 recognition mode.

claim: For the Cyclin B RNA, recognition of +6U is suboptimal and the +8U nucleotide is disordered in the ternary complex.
source: However, for the CycB RNA, recognition of +6U is suboptimal and the +8U nucleotide is disordered in the ternary complex (Figure 6E).
evidence: Crystal structure in Figure 6E shows disorder at +8U position.

claim: Nanos stabilizes binding of Pumilio to RNAs that do not match the PRE consensus sequence in the 3´ half, reducing Pumilio specificity to allow regulation of a broader range of mRNA targets than Pumilio alone.
source: Thus, Nos stabilizes binding of Pum to RNAs that do not match the PRE consensus sequence in the 3´ half, reducing Pum specificity to allow regulation of a broader range of mRNA targets than Pum alone.
evidence: Crystal structures and EMSA data show that Nos enables binding to divergent PREs like CycB.

claim: Pumilio alone reproducibly enriched a motif matching the PRE consensus in SEQRS analysis.
source: Pum alone reproducibly enriched a motif matching the PRE consensus (Figure 7B, Figure 7―figure supplement 1).
evidence: SEQRS data in Figure 7B shows the Pum motif UGUAAAUA.

claim: Addition of Nanos to immobilized Pumilio enriched A/U-rich sequences upstream of the 5´-UGUA of the PRE.
source: Strikingly, addition of Nos to immobilized Pum enriched A/U-rich sequences upstream of the 5´-UGUA of the PRE (Figure 7C, Figure 7―figure supplement 2, 3), consistent with Nos recognition of the NBS.
evidence: SEQRS data in Figure 7C shows enrichment of upstream A/U-rich sequences.

claim: Sequence selection at the 3´ end of the Pumilio motif weakened when Nanos was added.
source: Sequence selection at the 3´ end of the Pum motif weakened.
evidence: SEQRS data in Figure 7C shows reduced specificity at 3' end compared to Figure 7B.

claim: The Nos-Pum motif was highly enriched by the wild-type ternary complex, whereas Nanos alone or the RNA-binding defective Pumilio did not enrich either motif.
source: Comparison of control SEQRS analyses demonstrated specificity of the interactions. The Pum motif was highly enriched by wild-type Pum alone and, to a lesser degree, in the presence of Nos (Figure 7D), the Nos-Pum motif was highly enriched by the wild-type ternary complex, whereas Nos alone or the RNA-binding defective Pum did not enrich either motif.
evidence: SEQRS data in Figure 7D shows motif enrichment specificity.

claim: The Nos-Pum motif and, to a lesser degree, the Pum motif, are enriched in Pumilio target mRNAs from both embryos and adults.
source: We examined whether the Nos-Pum motif was enriched in Pum target mRNAs identified from Drosophila embryos and adults (Gerber et al., 2006) and observed enrichment of the Nos-Pum motif and, to a lesser degree, the Pum motif, in targets from both embryos and adults (Figure 7E, Figure 7―figure supplement 4).
evidence: Analysis in Figure 7E shows enrichment of both motifs in Pum target mRNAs with citation to Gerber et al., 2006.

claim: More Pumilio target mRNAs bear the Nos-Pum motif than the Pum motif.
source: More Pum target mRNAs bear the Nos-Pum motif than the Pum motif, indicating that Nos expands the range of mRNAs regulated by Pum.
evidence: Analysis in Figure 7E shows higher percentage of mRNAs with Nos-Pum motif.

claim: Few mRNAs have consensus PREs with upstream NBS motifs (i.e. both Nos-Pum and Pum motifs), such as hunchback mRNA.
source: Notably, few mRNAs have consensus PREs with upstream NBS motifs (i.e. both Nos-Pum and Pum motifs), such as hb mRNA.
evidence: Analysis in Figure 7E and Figure 7-figure supplement 4 shows small overlap between motifs.

claim: Most mRNAs with Pum motifs lack the upstream NBS, suggesting that they may be targeted by Pumilio alone or with other partners.
source: Most mRNAs with Pum motifs lack the upstream NBS, suggesting that they may be targeted by Pum alone or with other partners.
evidence: Analysis in Figure 7E and Figure 7-figure supplement 4 shows many mRNAs with only Pum motif.

claim: Gene ontology analyses of target mRNAs bearing Pum or Nos-Pum motifs show significantly enriched terms that match the known functions of Nanos and Pumilio, including body pattern formation and germline development.
source: Finally, we performed gene ontology analyses of target mRNAs bearing Pum or Nos-Pum motifs and observed that significantly enriched terms match the known functions of Nos and Pum, including body pattern formation and germline development, and also suggest new collaborative functions including regulation of cell division, receptor protein signaling, and cell fate determination (Figure 7F).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis in Figure 7F shows enrichment of these terms.

claim: Gene ontology analyses suggest new collaborative functions of Nanos and Pumilio including regulation of cell division, receptor protein signaling, and cell fate determination.
source: Finally, we performed gene ontology analyses of target mRNAs bearing Pum or Nos-Pum motifs and observed that significantly enriched terms match the known functions of Nos and Pum, including body pattern formation and germline development, and also suggest new collaborative functions including regulation of cell division, receptor protein signaling, and cell fate determination (Figure 7F).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis in Figure 7F shows enrichment of these terms.

claim: Nanos-enhanced repression of the 1x hunchback NRE2 reporter was dose dependent, increasing from 12% with 1 ng of transfected Nanos expression vector to 68% with 200 ng.
source: We found that Nos-enhanced repression of the 1x hb NRE2 reporter was dose dependent, increasing from 12% with 1 ng of transfected Nos expression vector to 68% with 200 ng (Figure 8C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C shows dose-dependent repression.

claim: Nanos elicited dose-dependent repression of reporters bearing the 1x hunchback NRE1 or bicoid NRE.
source: Nos also elicited dose-dependent repression of reporters bearing the 1x hb NRE1 or bcd NRE, which were not stably bound by Pum alone, but supported ternary complex formation.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C shows dose-dependent repression of these reporters.

claim: The Nanos gradient did not enhance repression of reporters bearing the 1x Cyclin B NRE or 1x hunchback NRE2 +3G mutant, relative to the background repression of a control reporter lacking a PRE.
source: In contrast, the Nos gradient did not enhance repression of reporters bearing the 1x CycB NRE or 1x hb NRE2 +3G mutant, relative to the background repression of a control reporter lacking a PRE (MCS) or the 1x hb NRE2 ACA mutant that abrogated Pum binding and ternary complex formation.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C shows no significant repression above background for these reporters.

claim: 10 ng of transfected Nanos expression vector resulted in 79% repression for the 3x hunchback NRE2 reporter versus 45% repression for the 1x hunchback NRE2 reporter.
source: To improve the signal-to-noise ratio, we increased the number of NREs in each reporter to three adjacent sites, which dramatically increased cellular repression with lower amounts of Nos expression: 10 ng of transfected Nos expression vector resulted in 79% repression for the 3x hb NRE2 reporter (Figure 8D) versus 45% repression for the 1x hb NRE2 reporter (Figure 8C).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C and 8D shows increased repression with 3x NREs.

claim: Nanos-enhanced repression of the 3x Cyclin B NRE and mutant hunchback NRE2 +3G reporters was dose-dependent and significantly above background.
source: Nos-enhanced repression of the 3x CycB NRE and mutant hb NRE2 +3G reporters was dose-dependent and significantly above background (Figure 8D).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8D shows dose-dependent repression above background.

claim: Multiple weak NREs, such as 3x Cyclin B NRE or 3x hunchback NRE2 +3G, confer substantial repression that approaches the level of a single strong NRE.
source: Thus, Nos enhances cellular repression of mRNAs with NREs that diverge from the PRE consensus and do not form stable complexes with Pum alone. Moreover, multiple weak NREs, such as 3x CycB NRE or 3x hb NRE2 +3G, confer substantial repression that approaches the level of a single strong NRE (e.g. 1x hb NRE2).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C and 8D shows that 3x weak NREs achieve repression levels approaching 1x strong NRE.

claim: Nanos appears to expand the Pumilio target mRNA repertoire beyond those with perfect 5´-UGUAHAUA core PRE consensus sequences by stabilizing Nos-Pum-RNA complexes.
source: As a consequence, Nos appears to expand the Pum target mRNA repertoire beyond those with perfect 5´-UGUAHAUA core PRE consensus sequences by stabilizing Nos-Pum-RNA complexes.
evidence: EMSA and reporter assay data show that Nos enables regulation of divergent PREs.

claim: The addition of Nanos and the upstream nucleotides induces localized conformational changes in Pumilio that promote Nos-Pum interaction and binding of Pumilio to RNA upstream of the core PRE site.
source: Comparison of the ternary and binary complexes reveals that the addition of Nos and the upstream nucleotides induces localized conformational changes in Pum that promote Nos-Pum interaction and binding of Pum to RNA upstream of the core PRE site.
evidence: Crystal structures in Figure 2-figure supplement 2 show conformational changes in Pum.

claim: Loop residues between Pumilio repeats R7 and R8 rearrange in the ternary complex to promote interaction of F1367Pum with the C-terminal α helix of Nanos.
source: Loop residues between repeats R7 and R8 rearrange in the ternary complex to promote interaction of F1367Pum with the C-terminal α helix of Nos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Crystal structure in Figure 2-figure supplement 2 shows this rearrangement.

claim: The C-terminal α helix of Pumilio (helix α2 of repeat R8´) unfolds to promote interaction of residues with the upstream RNA backbone.
source: In addition, the C-terminal α helix of Pum (helix α2 of repeat R8´) unfolds to promote interaction of residues with the upstream RNA backbone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Crystal structure in Figure 2-figure supplement 2 and 2-figure supplement 3 shows this unfolding.

claim: The Nanos-Pumilio interface and phylogenetic comparisons indicate that the Drosophila Nos-Pum interaction is conserved among Dipteran orthologs.
source: Based on our current understanding of the Pum-Nos interface and phylogenetic comparisons, the Drosophila Nos-Pum interaction is conserved among Dipteran orthologs, but it is not possible to predict conservation of the interaction in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated based on phylogenetic analysis of the interface residues.

claim: It is not possible to predict conservation of the Drosophila Nos-Pum interaction in vertebrates.
source: Based on our current understanding of the Pum-Nos interface and phylogenetic comparisons, the Drosophila Nos-Pum interaction is conserved among Dipteran orthologs, but it is not possible to predict conservation of the interaction in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated based on divergence of interface residues in vertebrates.

claim: The Nanos C-terminal region that contacts Pumilio is conserved within Diptera, but substantially diverges beyond that order.
source: The Nos C-terminal region that contacts Pum is conserved within Diptera, but substantially diverges beyond that order (Curtis et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Vertebrates have three Nanos orthologs which share the tandem Nos zinc fingers but diverge substantially in their C termini.
source: Vertebrates have three Nos orthologs which share the tandem Nos ZFs but diverge substantially in their C termini.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of vertebrate Nos proteins.

claim: The C termini of human Nanos proteins are not homologous to each other or Drosophila Nanos.
source: For example, the C termini of human Nos proteins are not homologous to each other or Drosophila Nos.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: The contacts points observed in the Nos-Pum structure are conserved in Dipteran orthologs, but diverge throughout the tree of life.
source: We also analyzed the conservation of the Nos-binding interface of Pum proteins and find that the contacts points observed in the Nos-Pum structure are conserved in Dipteran orthologs, but diverge throughout the tree of life.
evidence: This is stated based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Residues equivalent to Pumilio Q1337 and F1367 change to proline and methionine, respectively, in vertebrate Pum homologs.
source: For example, residues equivalent to Pum Q1337 and F1367 change to proline and methionine, respectively, in vertebrate Pum homologs.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: Vertebrate PUM proteins possess a three residue (GPH) insertion in the R7-R8 loop region that could augment protein contacts with vertebrate Nos proteins.
source: In addition, vertebrate PUM proteins possess a three residue (GPH) insertion in the R7-R8 loop region that could augment protein contacts with vertebrate Nos proteins.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: Deletion of the GPH residues allows human Pum1 to interact with Drosophila Nanos.
source: Interestingly, deletion of these residues allows human Pum1 to interact with Drosophila Nos (Sonoda and Wharton, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Nanos and Pumilio homologs from C. elegans, Xenopus and humans have been reported to interact.
source: First, the direct interaction between Drosophila Nos and Pum might be unique to Dipterans; however, Nos and Pum homologs from C. elegans, Xenopus and humans have been reported to interact and a simple loop deletion allows human Pum1 to interact with Drosophila Nos (Jaruzelska et al., 2003; Kraemer et al., 1999; Lolicato et al., 2008; Nakahata et al., 2001; Sonoda and Wharton 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The Nanos and Pumilio contacts likely coevolved as the number of Nos and Pum homologs increased, perhaps restricting interactions between particular Nos and Pum proteins.
source: Instead, the Nos and Pum contacts likely coevolved as the number of Nos and Pum homologs increased, perhaps restricting interactions between particular Nos and Pum proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: Nanos and Pumilio homologs may also interact indirectly, mediated by a bridging partner(s), as was suggested for C. elegans and mouse.
source: Nos and Pum homologs may also interact indirectly, mediated by a bridging partner(s), as was suggested for C. elegans (Kraemer et al., 1999) and mouse (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Nanos specifically recognizes the 5´ sequence only in the context of the ternary complex.
source: Nos specifically recognizes the 5´ sequence only in the context of the ternary complex and also induces a localized conformational change of Pum that adds contacts with the phosphate backbone of nucleotides -1 to -4.
evidence: Crystal structures and EMSA data show that Nos does not bind RNA alone but recognizes specific sequences in the ternary complex.

claim: Previous reports indicated that the Nanos tandem zinc fingers in isolation exhibit non-specific RNA binding.
source: Previous reports indicated that the Nos tandem ZFs in isolation exhibit non-specific RNA binding (Curtis et al., 1997; Hashimoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The mutations in the RNAs tested by Curtis et al. were outside the Nanos binding site and thus would not have detected sequence-specific differences in Nanos binding.
source: With our structure-based definition of the NBS, we find that the mutations in the RNAs tested by Curtis et al. were outside the NBS and thus would not have detected sequence-specific differences in Nos binding.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of the NBS definition with previous studies.

claim: The negative effect of NBS mutations on abdominal segmentation in vivo can be attributed to the loss of RNA recognition by Nanos.
source: With our findings, we can now attribute the negative effect of NBS mutations on abdominal segmentation in vivo (Wharton et al., 1998) and ternary complex formation in yeast three-hybrid assays (Sonoda and Wharton, 1999) to the loss of RNA recognition by Nos.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Cooperative RNA recognition by Nanos and Pumilio is reminiscent of cooperative binding of msl2 RNA by Sex lethal (Sxl) and Upstream of N-Ras (Unr).
source: Cooperative RNA recognition by Nos and Pum is reminiscent of cooperative binding of msl2 RNA by Sex lethal (Sxl) and Upstream of N-Ras (Unr) (Hennig et al., 2014), yet the mechanisms and effects of cooperative recognition by Nos and Pum display novel distinguishing characteristics.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Similar to Nanos and Pumilio, Sex lethal and Unr proteins interact with each other only in the presence of target RNA, cooperatively interacting with a regulatory element that contains binding sites for each protein.
source: Similar to Nos and Pum, Sxl and Unr proteins interact with each other only in the presence of target RNA, cooperatively interacting with a regulatory element that contains binding sites for each protein.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the Sxl-Unr system.

claim: Sex lethal and Unr recognize the RNA nucleotides between their individual binding sites, forming a sandwich or a 'triple zipper' arrangement that creates a longer recognition element than either protein alone.
source: Sxl and Unr recognize the RNA nucleotides between their individual binding sites, forming a sandwich or a "triple zipper" arrangement that creates a longer recognition element than either protein alone.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the Sxl-Unr system.

claim: Nanos recognition of the 5´ NBS and clamp-like binding to Pumilio and RNA relaxes the sequence requirements of Pumilio interaction with the 3´ end of the PRE, effectively shifting the recognition sequence, rather than extending it.
source: Nos and Pum recognize their respective NBS and PRE elements; however, Nos recognition of the 5´ NBS and clamp-like binding to Pum and RNA relaxes the sequence requirements of Pum interaction with the 3´ end of the PRE, as with CycB mRNA, which effectively shifts the recognition sequence, rather than extending it.
evidence: SEQRS and structural data show relaxed 3' specificity and shifted recognition.

claim: Nanos and Pumilio cooperatively bind to RNAs that neither protein stably binds on its own.
source: As a consequence, Nos and Pum cooperatively bind to RNAs that neither protein stably binds on its own.
evidence: EMSA data shows that Nos enables binding to RNAs like CycB NRE that Pum alone does not bind.

claim: The majority of Pumilio target mRNAs contain the Nos-Pum motif but lack the full canonical PRE Pumilio recognition sequence.
source: Our analysis of Pum target mRNAs using the SEQRS-derived Nos-Pum motif indicates that the majority of Pum target mRNAs contain the Nos-Pum motif but lack the full canonical PRE Pum recognition sequence.
evidence: Analysis in Figure 7E shows higher prevalence of Nos-Pum motif in target mRNAs.

claim: In addition to strengthening Pumilio repression activity, Nanos can alter the identity of mRNAs regulated by Pumilio.
source: This suggests that, in addition to strengthening Pum repression activity, Nos can alter the identity of mRNAs regulated by Pum.
evidence: SEQRS and motif analysis show different target mRNA populations.

claim: Enrichment of specific gene ontology terms in the mRNAs bearing the Nos-Pum motif suggest that Nanos can alter the biological functions controlled by Pumilio.
source: Moreover, enrichment of specific gene ontology terms in the mRNAs bearing the Nos-Pum motif suggest that Nos can alter the biological functions controlled by Pum (Figure 7).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis in Figure 7F shows different enriched terms for Nos-Pum vs Pum motifs.

claim: Repression is responsive to the Nanos protein concentration.
source: In addition to altering sequence specificity, our studies highlight other advantages of combinatorial RNA target regulation by Nos and Pum in vivo. First, repression is responsive to the Nos protein concentration.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C-D shows dose-dependent repression.

claim: In the Drosophila embryo, the Nanos protein gradient is highest at the posterior end where hunchback expression must be repressed for abdomen formation.
source: In the Drosophila embryo, the Nos protein gradient is highest at the posterior end where hb expression must be repressed for abdomen formation (Barker et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Higher Nanos levels induced greater repression of reporters bearing hunchback NREs, mirroring the effect in the embryonic posterior.
source: We showed that higher Nos levels induced greater repression of reporters bearing hb NREs, mirroring the effect in the embryonic posterior.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C shows dose-dependent repression.

claim: The expression of Nanos is dynamic over the course of development and likely modulates Pumilio activity temporally as well as spatially.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Nos is dynamic over the course of development and likely modulates Pum activity temporally as well as spatially (Wang and Lehmann, 1991).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Repression is affected by the sequence of the NREs; reporters bearing imperfect PREs were also repressed, but required higher Nanos protein levels for equivalent effect.
source: Second, repression is affected by the sequence of the NREs; reporters bearing imperfect PREs were also repressed, but required higher Nos protein levels for equivalent effect.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C-D shows different dose-response curves for different NRE sequences.

claim: The number of Nos-Pum binding sites in the mRNA modulates regulatory activity.
source: Third, the number of Nos-Pum binding sites in the mRNA modulates regulatory activity.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C-D shows increased repression with 3x NREs vs 1x NREs.

claim: Hunchback mRNA bears two NREs, each with consensus NBS and PRE sites.
source: For example, hb mRNA bears two NREs, each with consensus NBS and PRE sites.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of hb mRNA.

claim: Each hunchback NRE site was highly responsive to Nanos-enhanced, Pumilio-mediated repression, and multiple sites conferred greater responsiveness.
source: We found that each site was highly responsive to Nos-enhanced, Pum-mediated repression, and multiple sites conferred greater responsiveness.
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 1C shows repression with single and double NREs.

claim: Repression of the Cyclin B PRE reporter required higher concentrations of transfected Nanos, mirroring the requirement for concentrated Nanos protein in pole cells where Cyclin B translation is repressed.
source: Repression of the CycB PRE reporter required higher concentrations of transfected Nos, mirroring the requirement for concentrated Nos protein in pole cells where CycB translation is repressed (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999; Kadyrova et al., 2007).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8C-D shows higher Nos requirement for CycB NRE, with supporting citations.

claim: Inclusion of three Cyclin B PREs supported repression at lower Nanos concentrations.
source: Inclusion of three CycB PREs supported repression at lower Nos concentrations, consistent with previous studies showing how the number and quality of PREs in the hb 3´UTR, and the amount of Nos protein expressed, confer the precise level of regulation upon the hb transcript in embryonic development (Wharton and Struhl, 1991).
evidence: Reporter assay data in Figure 8D shows repression with 3x CycB NREs at lower Nos concentrations, with supporting citation.

claim: The Cyclin B mRNA 3´ UTR contains no perfect PRE, but it does contain 7 sequence elements with an NBS upstream of a partial PRE with the 5´ UGU sequence.
source: Indeed, although the CycB mRNA 3´ UTR contains no perfect PRE, it does contain 7 sequence elements with an NBS upstream of a partial PRE with the 5´ UGU sequence.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis of CycB mRNA.

claim: The Brain Tumor (Brat) protein contributes to repression of hunchback expression in the embryo by recognizing an element located upstream of the NBS and PRE in each NRE.
source: For example, the Brain Tumor (Brat) protein contributes to repression of hb expression in the embryo by recognizing an element located upstream of the NBS and PRE in each NRE (i.e. the so-called Box A motif) (Laver et al., 2015; Loedige et al., 2014; Sonoda and Wharton, 2001).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Additional partner proteins can modulate RNA binding of PUF proteins.
source: Moreover, additional partner proteins can modulate RNA binding of PUF proteins (Campbell et al., 2012a, 2012b; Menichelli et al., 2013) and the Nos-Pum-RNA ternary complex suggests common mechanisms of co-regulation.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: RNA-binding affinity and specificity of the C. elegans PUF protein, FBF-2, is modulated by interactions with CPB-1 (Cytoplasmic Polyadenylation element Binding protein 1).
source: For instance, RNA-binding affinity and specificity of the C. elegans PUF protein, FBF-2, is modulated by interactions with CPB-1 (Cytoplasmic Polyadenylation element Binding protein 1) (Menichelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: CPB-1 and other partners bind to a region of FBF-2 that corresponds to the R7-R8 loop of Pumilio that binds Nanos.
source: Intriguingly, CPB-1 and other partners bind to a region of FBF-2 that corresponds to the R7-R8 loop of Pum that binds Nos (Campbell et al., 2012b; Menichelli et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The Nos-Pum-RNA complex exemplifies a protein-protein interaction hotspot.
source: Thus, the Nos-Pum-RNA complex exemplifies a protein-protein interaction hotspot (Campbell et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Formation of PUF protein-partner complexes can alter the PUF protein conformation to create additional protein-RNA contacts that strengthen RNA binding while modulating target specificity and regulation.
source: Our results indicate that formation of PUF protein-partner complexes can alter the PUF protein conformation to create additional protein-RNA contacts that strengthen RNA binding while modulating target specificity and regulation.
evidence: Crystal structures and binding data show conformational changes and altered specificity.

claim: Nanos ZF2 is strikingly similar to the HIV nucleocapsid protein zinc knuckles.
source: However, we manually compared the Nos ZFs with CCHC Zn knuckles (ZKs) from HIV nucleocapsid protein (HIVnc) (De Guzman et al., 1998) and found that Nos ZF2 is strikingly similar to the HIVnc ZKs (Figure 9).
evidence: Structural comparison in Figure 9 shows similarity between Nos ZF2 and HIVnc ZK2.

claim: The N-terminal region of Nanos increases repression by the Nos-Pum complex by recruiting the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex.
source: Protein interaction modules may also strengthen regulation by enhancing recruitment of cofactors. The N-terminal region of Nos, not included in our crystal structures, increases repression by the Nos-Pum complex by recruiting the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex (Kadyrova et al., 2007; Raisch et al., 2016), which strengthens the independent repression activity of Pum (Weidmann et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex strengthens the independent repression activity of Pumilio.
source: Protein interaction modules may also strengthen regulation by enhancing recruitment of cofactors. The N-terminal region of Nos, not included in our crystal structures, increases repression by the Nos-Pum complex by recruiting the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex (Kadyrova et al., 2007; Raisch et al., 2016), which strengthens the independent repression activity of Pum (Weidmann et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The nosL7 mutant allele causes a lethal loss of abdominal segments during embryogenesis and encodes a Nanos protein with a deletion of residues 376–382 near the C terminus.
source: One of the first nos mutant alleles identified, nosL7, causes a lethal loss of abdominal segments during embryogenesis and encodes a Nos protein with a deletion of residues 376–382 near the C terminus (Arrizabalaga and Lehmann, 1999; Lehmann, 1988).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The nosL7 deletion prevents formation of a Nos-Pum-RNA complex as assessed by yeast three-hybrid and in vitro pull-down assays.
source: This deletion prevents formation of a Nos-Pum-RNA complex as assessed by yeast three-hybrid and in vitro pull-down assays (Sonoda and Wharton, 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Insertion of four residues in the R7-R8 loop in the PumMlu mutant disrupts complex formation, hunchback repression and abdominal segmentation.
source: In addition, F1367Pum is within the loop between Pum repeats R7 and R8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), explaining why insertion of four residues in the R7-R8 loop in the PumMlu mutant disrupts complex formation, hb repression and abdominal segmentation (Sonoda and Wharton, 1999; Wharton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.
